subject: Vocabulary
description: Common English proverbs + their meanings; SSC PYQ favourites

questions.stem: Meaning of proverb 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE':

options.option_text: Sewing carefully takes time and effort here
Acting promptly prevents larger trouble later
Wear nine layers of clothing always for warmth
Stitch nine pieces of cloth together as one

questions.explanation: A small + timely action prevents bigger problems later. Origin: small tear in cloth needs only 1 stitch now; left alone, it grows + needs 9. Applies broadly: maintenance > repair, prevention > cure. Common parallel: 'A penny saved is a penny earned'; 'an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure'.

questions.stem: Meaning of proverb 'EMPTY VESSELS MAKE THE MOST NOISE':

options.option_text: Loud places have empty containers
Foolish or shallow people talk most
Quiet people are not knowledgeable
Containers should be filled fully

questions.explanation: Empty / shallow people often boast loudly + show off; truly knowledgeable people are quieter / more humble. Origin: striking an empty pot makes loud sound; a full pot is dull. Comparable: 'Still waters run deep' (quiet people may be deep); 'Half-knowledge is dangerous'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'BIRDS OF A FEATHER FLOCK TOGETHER' means:

options.option_text: Birds need feathers to fly always
People of similar nature stay together
Flocks of birds migrate seasonally
Birds prefer to live in colonies

questions.explanation: People with similar interests, character, or background tend to associate. Used positively or with caution (your friends reflect on you). Origin: birds of same species naturally flock. Compare: 'Tell me your friends, I'll tell you who you are'; 'You are the company you keep'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'A ROLLING STONE GATHERS NO MOSS' means:

options.option_text: Stones are smooth in flowing rivers
Constant change prevents stability + gain
Moss grows only on still surfaces
Stones never accumulate any growth

questions.explanation: Original meaning: a person who keeps changing jobs, places, partners doesn't accumulate wealth, friends, or settled life. Modern usage = sometimes positive (staying free + flexible), but traditionally negative. Origin: ancient Latin (Publius Syrus) — 'Saxum volutum non obducitur musco'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'STRIKE WHILE THE IRON IS HOT' means:

options.option_text: Hit metal only when it's heated
Act when conditions are favourable
Iron is dangerous at high heat
Forge iron tools for daily use

questions.explanation: Take advantage of an opportunity at the right moment. Origin: blacksmith metaphor — iron is malleable only when hot; let it cool + you can't shape it. Modern usage: 'Strike while iron is hot' = act now, opportunity won't last. Similar: 'Make hay while the sun shines'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'WHEN IN ROME, DO AS THE ROMANS DO' means:

options.option_text: Always travel to Rome historically
Adapt to customs of the place you're in
Follow Roman customs strictly always
Romans were the original culture-makers

questions.explanation: When you're in a new place, follow / respect the local customs. Origin: St. Ambrose advised St. Augustine — 'When at Rome, live in Roman style; when elsewhere, live as elsewhere live'. Practical wisdom: cultural sensitivity. Often quoted in business + travel contexts.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'TOO MANY COOKS SPOIL THE BROTH' means:

options.option_text: Cooks need to learn skills more
Excess people in a task ruin it
Broth is hard to make tasty
Cooks should always work alone

questions.explanation: Too many people involved in a single task → confusion + conflicting ideas → poor outcome. Origin: kitchen metaphor — multiple cooks each adding their own thing → spoiled broth. Modern parallels: too many decision-makers, design-by-committee. Counter-proverb: 'Many hands make light work' (when tasks are divisible) — different contexts.
